title: Why You Must Tell Your Students WHY
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Using a personal anecdote about a diverted flight and an unreasonably rigid airport security guard, Linsin argues that rules enforced without an explained reason breed the same resentment in students that arbitrary authority breeds in adults. His central claim is that a "compelling reason" is simply whatever is genuinely best for the students, explained in terms they can understand — and that offering this explanation is what separates grudging compliance from real buy-in. He contrasts the guard's dismissive "you don't need to know" with how differently people respond when the reasoning behind a restriction is made clear, arguing the same psychology governs a classroom. The concrete takeaway is behavioral: before enforcing any rule, expectation, or policy, a teacher should be able to articulate why it serves students, not just the teacher's convenience or authority. He closes by claiming that when students trust a rule exists for their own benefit, they relax, focus better, and the relationship with the teacher becomes measurably more influential.
points: Rules enforced without an explained reason are said to provoke the same resentment in students that arbitrary authority provokes in adults.
A "compelling reason" is defined narrowly as whatever is genuinely best for students, explained in language they understand.
Explaining the why is credited with producing eager buy-in rather than mere grudging compliance.
Students are said to relax and focus better once they trust a rule serves their benefit rather than the teacher's convenience.
quotes: If this has ever happened to you, then you know how hard it is to nod off amidst the cleaning crew’s toils and blaring announcements over the intercom.
His answer: “Because I’m the security guard and you don’t need to know.
In other words, it was arbitrary. This, of course, infuriated the horde, who one after the other trudged back to the gate muttering indecents under their breath.
If you don’t have a compelling reason why you do, well, everything—though especially your rules, expectations, and policies—then you shouldn’t do it.
So what is a compelling reason? Whatever is best for students, which then must be explained to them in a way they understand.
The result is better motivation and a more influential relationship with your class.
